title: Garmin put GPS on your wrist. Why couldn't you just run?｜Brand Story
description:
Putting GPS on your wrist doesn't automatically mean recording a run well. Starting with the Forerunner 201, shipped in November 2003, we follow charging and initial satellite acquisition, pace smoothing and a target partner, history storage and serial-port transfers. Then come the wrist-side antennas, chest-strap IDs and recording capacity of the 2006 205/305, followed by how a long-term user handled the data in 2009.

The 201 manual is February 2006 Rev F; the 205/305 manual is Rev D, ©2006–2008. Later manuals cannot all be treated as launch firmware. The 15–30 minutes applies only to the 201's initial position fix; 3.5 hours is the 305's detailed-data capacity when recording every second. DC Rainmaker's original post dates to 2007, but this video uses his account explicitly marked as substantially updated on 2009-06-25, not a controlled accuracy experiment. It excludes the dynamic comparison table, reader comments and swimming advice. Phone competition is not presented as the reason the 2003 running watch was invented. Visuals are anonymous conceptual illustrations.

chapters.gr1h01: The watch on your wrist waits for the sky
chapters.gr1s01: Charge first, then wait for the signal bar to vanish
chapters.gr1r01: Save this run before the next reset
chapters.gr1a01: An antenna curves around the wrist toward the sky

gr1h01.text: Outside, you hold down the Forerunner 201's power button. The satellite icon is still flashing.

gr1h03.text: If this is your first position fix, the wait could stretch to 15–30 minutes.

gr1h02.text: These are the steps before your first run in the manual revised in February 2006.

gr1h04.text: The battery is charged and you're ready. What is the watch on your wrist still waiting for?

gr1h05.text: Once you start running, the two little figures on the screen will raise another question.

gr1h06.text: By 2006, another device first had to deal with your constantly swinging arm.

gr1h07.text: We'll follow Garmin's changes, from finding your position to keeping a record, along this journey of wrist-worn GPS.

gr1h08.text: Once GPS is on your wrist, what else does it need to become a running tool you can actually use?

gr1s01.text: To leave a record of your run, our starting point is this device, first shipped in November 2003.

gr1s02.text: The company's annual report that year described speed, time, distance and lap times while running.

gr1s03.text: The preliminary specifications listed its weight as 78 grams.

gr1s04.text: Its rectangular body was over 8 centimeters wide and less than 2 centimeters thick.

gr1s05.text: If you wanted to read it while running, the whole device, display included, had to stay on your wrist.

gr1s06.text: It reached runners' wrists well before car navigation later faced competition from phones.

gr1s07.text: When you took this device outside, where would its power come from?

gr1s08.text: It used a rechargeable lithium battery. The manual listed up to 15 hours of use on a full charge.

gr1s09.text: The later revised manual also warned that cold, heat and battery aging would all reduce available power.

gr1s10.text: So you dry the contacts, then clip the end with four contacts into the charging cradle first.

gr1s11.text: The revised manual says to charge it for at least two hours before first use.

gr1s12.text: A normal full charge is listed as taking between one and three hours.

gr1s13.text: But if it has sat unused until the battery is completely drained, will the screen always respond as soon as you plug it in?

gr1s14.text: The manual says that in this case, charging may take up to 30 minutes before it turns on or shows that it is charging.

gr1s15.text: So if the screen stays dark, you first need to work out whether it is still recovering its charge.

gr1s16.text: Once the power is in, how does the watch know where you're standing?

gr1s17.text: I find this starting point interesting: you already know where you are, but the machine doesn't.

gr1s18.text: That revised manual spells out the conditions for finding a signal quite precisely.

gr1s19.text: For first use, leave it somewhere with a clear view of the sky.

gr1s20.text: But do you have to wait that long every time you head out?

gr1s21.text: The earlier wait applies only to the initial position fix. The same page says later satellite acquisition usually takes less than a few minutes.

gr1s22.text: If you're in a hurry to get out for a run, those two waits are worlds apart.

gr1s23.text: But the watch is looking for signals from the sky, and roofs and buildings block its view.

gr1s24.text: How must that flashing satellite icon from the opening change before you press Start?

gr1s25.text: The satellite icon stops flashing and the signal bar disappears. Those are the signs that it has a position fix.

gr1s26.text: Only then do you press Start, and the watch begins timing and tracking distance.

gr1s28.text: But knowing your location alone doesn't tell you how that stretch of running went.

gr1p01.text: Time, pace and distance appear on the running watch's main workout screen.

gr1p02.text: Press the up and down buttons to switch to the current lap's pace, time and distance.

gr1p03.text: The same position data is now paired with time, becoming the progress a runner wants to see.

gr1p04.text: But if position and speed contain errors, how should you read the pace on the screen?

gr1p05.text: It offers a pace-smoothing setting that averages pace over a period of time.

gr1p06.text: The manual says this is intended to avoid errors in GPS position and speed calculations.

gr1p07.text: You can choose different smoothing levels, from strongest to weakest.

gr1p08.text: My next question would be: once you have pace, do you still have to do mental arithmetic to keep up with your goal?

gr1p10.text: Now those two little figures from the opening have a job.

gr1p11.text: First, enter the distance and time you want to run, so the device can create a goal.

gr1p12.text: Press Start, and the Virtual Partner at the top of the screen runs ahead according to that goal.

gr1p13.text: The figure below represents you, with the gap between you shown underneath.

gr1p14.text: Is the person you're chasing on the screen another real person?

gr1p15.text: What you're chasing here is your preset goal. There isn't another real person running online.

gr1p16.text: But runs can include red lights. Should the timer keep counting through them?

gr1p17.text: You can set it to pause the timer automatically when your pace drops below a chosen value.

gr1p18.text: When the pause condition is met, the timer indicator flashes.

gr1p19.text: That deals with time spent stopped. How can you record segments while moving?

gr1p20.text: A separate automatic lap function records a lap when you reach a set distance.

gr1p22.text: You can also press the Lap button yourself to tell it this segment ends here.

gr1p23.text: If you manually stop the timer and restart it, the device also automatically counts a new lap.

gr1p25.text: So after your run, can those segments and positions all be kept together?

gr1r01.text: Stop the timer, then hold Reset for three seconds. This run becomes your last run.

gr1r03.text: The manual says the device automatically saves the last run and its history data.

gr1r04.text: Reading this, I want to ask: does saving history mean every single point has survived?

gr1r06.text: The manual lists memory for up to 5,000 laps.

gr1r07.text: The ten most recent runs have basic tracks, while the latest run, not yet reset, is recorded in more detail.

gr1r08.text: The detailed track for that run can hold up to 3,000 points.

gr1r09.text: If you want to preserve the finest detail, before which action must you transfer it?

gr1r10.text: The manual reminds you to transfer it to a computer before the next reset. The receiver needs a connection at the other end.

gr1r11.text: The cradle used for charging now has to connect the device and the computer.

gr1r12.text: This time, the cradle's serial cable also plugs into the computer's serial port.

gr1r13.text: Open the training software and select Receive History to transfer the activity into it.

gr1r14.text: Once it's on the computer, does it end with a single look at the numbers?

gr1r15.text: In the training software, you can also add notes and export your running history as a data file.

gr1r16.text: If you want it to navigate you back, how detailed can the watch's map be?

gr1r17.text: You can turn on map mode to show the track you've followed.

gr1r18.text: It cannot load detailed map data. The screen mainly shows you and location points.

gr1r19.text: Choose a saved location to navigate to, and the device draws a straight line from your current position.

gr1r20.text: If there's an obstacle along that line, you still have to find your own way around it.

gr1r22.text: But with your arm constantly swinging, can the receiver keep a good view of the sky?

gr1a01.text: The 205 and 305 specifications state that the patch antenna faces the sky as your arm swings.

gr1a03.text: Looking back at the device previewed in our opening, Garmin says its antenna extended around part of the wrist.

gr1a04.text: That shape was intended to give the antenna a better view of the sky.

gr1a05.text: The way you raise your hand to read the screen and the direction the receiver needs to face have to be handled together.

gr1a06.text: At this point I'd ask: with a different receiver, do you still need to find satellites in an open area first?

gr1a07.text: The specifications also list a high-sensitivity receiver, but the manual doesn't tell you to start running straight away.

gr1a08.text: It still calls for an open area, away from tall buildings and trees, to acquire satellites.

gr1a09.text: Point the antenna upward, stand still and wait for the acquisition page to disappear.

gr1a11.text: If you want to know how hard your body is working, what data can you receive besides speed?

gr1a12.text: The heart-rate data added by the 305 comes from another item worn against your body.

gr1a13.text: The chest strap must touch your skin directly and sit just below the breastbone.

gr1a14.text: You also wet the two sensing patches on the back to connect your pulse to the transmitter.

gr1a15.text: The chest strap in this manual works with the 305. The same-generation 205 does not support it.

gr1a17.text: But once you've put the chest strap on, how does the watch know it's receiving your data?

gr1a18.text: Each sensor has its own identification code, which the watch learns during the first pairing.

gr1a19.text: The next time you turn it on, it uses that saved code to look for that sensor.

gr1a20.text: After pairing, the manual says it receives data only from that sensor.

gr1a21.text: How close must your watch and chest strap be during pairing to meet the manual's recommendation?

gr1a23.text: The manual says within three meters of each other, and away from other people's sensors.

gr1a24.text: If it seems to have paired with someone else's sensor, the troubleshooting advice is to scan again.

gr1a26.text: Once the signal is coming in, the storage still has to hold this run.

gr1a27.text: Keep every second, or just the important changes?

gr1d01.text: The 305's default Smart Recording selects key points based on changes in direction, speed or heart rate.

gr1d03.text: If you switch to recording every second, can it keep the entire activity indefinitely?

gr1d04.text: But the manual goes on to say that this allows at most 3.5 hours of detailed data.

gr1d06.text: That is a storage limit for detailed data. Battery endurance is a separate specification.

gr1d07.text: I see it as a new trade-off within the same run: not every point can be kept forever.

gr1d08.text: The manual also warns that when history is full, older data is automatically overwritten.

gr1d09.text: To guard against overwriting, it recommends regularly transferring history to a computer for safekeeping.

gr1d10.text: What can an activity saved in history do for your next outing?

gr1d11.text: You can choose an activity from history and use it to create a course.

gr1d12.text: Run along it again, and your goal can become matching that earlier performance.

gr1d14.text: If you want prompts for a water stop or turn, you can also add course points.

gr1d15.text: But those course points must be added in the training software on a computer.

gr1d16.text: Only after you transfer them back to the device does the screen show the distance to the next course point.

gr1d17.text: But on one course, how can you see both yourself and that earlier activity?

gr1d18.text: The gray triangle on the map represents the progress of the original activity.

gr1d19.text: The black triangle is your current position.

gr1d20.text: If you stray off course, the arrow first guides you back. Where does it point once you're back?

gr1d21.text: Only once you're back on the course does the arrow resume showing which way to follow it.

gr1d24.text: The specifications let you compare with the past. After long-term running in practice, what actually remains?

gr1v02.text: That is his account in the long-term review he substantially updated on June 25, 2009.

gr1v03.text: Did the recordings he reported also suffer interruptions near obstructions?

gr1v04.text: He wrote that ordinary trees and lower buildings generally caused little trouble.

gr1v05.text: But running alongside taller buildings sometimes caused brief connection losses.

gr1v06.text: As for those little figures chasing a goal, did he use them to guide his own training?

gr1v07.text: In fact, he didn't use the little figures on the screen very much.

gr1v08.text: Because he trained mainly by heart rate, he looked more often at his body's response.

gr1v09.text: I think that's a practical choice: you don't have to chase every kind of data a device can display.

gr1v10.text: Does the same activity necessarily become easier to read once it's plotted on a computer?

gr1v11.text: He showed an example in which the pace for a single second suddenly produced a very high spike.

gr1v12.text: In the bundled software at the time, he couldn't edit data points or adjust the chart scale.

gr1v13.text: If you want to name and group each of your runs, how do you do that?

gr1v14.text: He wrote that he had switched to third-party software that could name, group and export the data.

gr1v15.text: If you want to compare two activities, how you organize the records matters too.

gr1f07.text: What that wait in the opening must ultimately give you is an activity you can understand and preserve.

gr1f08.text: If you keep running records, tell me in the comments: which measure do you look back at most often?

gr1f09.text: And subscribe, so we can keep explaining the designs whose results are usually all we see.
